analysis.investment_thesis: Electronics Mart India fails virtually every quantitative screen I require — P/E of 44x (nearly 3× my ceiling of 15), P/B of 2.6x (above my 1.5x limit), and Debt/Equity of 1.26 (over twice my 0.5 maximum). The Graham Number of approximately INR 62 (√(22.5 × ₹4.16 EPS × ₹40.4 BVPS)) reveals the stock trades at a ~70% premium to the only price I consider safe.
key_strengths: Consistent revenue growth — 17% CAGR over 5 years reaching ₹6,965 Cr, demonstrating the business can grow
Unbroken positive earnings history across 6 years (2020–2025), satisfying my minimum earnings continuity test
Interest coverage ratio of ~3.8x (EBIT ₹451 Cr / Finance Cost ₹118 Cr) — barely clears my 3.5x floor
key_risks: Dangerous leverage — borrowings exploded from ₹872 Cr (2020) to ₹1,963 Cr (2025), D/E of 1.26 leaves no margin in a downturn
Free cash flow deeply negative: –₹159 Cr (2025), –₹247 Cr (2023); capex of ₹335 Cr in 2025 consumes all operating cash and more
Razor-thin 4% operating margins in a commoditised retail business — any revenue softness or rate rise collapses profits
red_flags: P/E of 44x — priced for perfection in a low-margin, capital-intensive retailer
Net profit declined from ₹184 Cr (2024) to ₹160 Cr (2025) even as revenue grew — margin compression is accelerating
Finance costs compounding at 13.4% CAGR; if rates rise or expansion stalls, interest burden becomes existential
No dividend income — shareholders receive no current return while bearing substantial debt risk
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my perspective, Electronics Mart is a business I can understand but cannot buy at any price resembling today's. The Graham Number of roughly INR 62 — computed from trailing EPS of ₹4.16 and book value of ₹40.4 per share — places intrinsic value 41% below the current price of ₹105. Every valuation ratio offends my discipline: P/E of 44x, P/B of 2.6x. Mr. Market is asking me to pay for a rosy future in a business with 4% operating margins and a debt load that has more than doubled in five years. That is speculation, not investment.

The balance sheet concerns me most. Borrowings of ₹1,963 Cr against equity of ₹1,557 Cr means creditors have a larger claim on this business than shareholders do. The company burned ₹159 Cr of free cash in FY25 on store expansion — an aggressive bet that requires sustained consumer spending, low interest rates, and flawless execution. History shows that retailers who over-lever during expansion cycles suffer acutely in contractions. With declining net profit (₹184 Cr → ₹160 Cr in one year) and rising finance costs (₹118 Cr, up 13.4% annually), the earnings cushion is shrinking precisely when the debt pile is growing. I require a margin of safety; this stock offers none.
